artworks.title: Oenomaus and Myrtilus
artworks.description: This relief photograph preserves the chariot household of Pisa: King Oenomaus with his driver Myrtilus, son of Hermes — the charioteer whose sabotage (or betrayal) lets Pelops win Hippodamia. The image is a key visual witness to the figure whose curse, after Pelops hurled him into the sea, named the Myrtoan Sea and poisoned the Pelopid line.

artworks.title: Death of Myrtilus (Etruscan cinerary urn)
artworks.description: An Etruscan cinerary urn stages Pelops casting Myrtilus from the chariot — the murder that turns the helpful (or treacherous) driver into a dying curse. Carved in the second century BC for a Volterran tomb, the relief shows how central the charioteer's fall was to Italic reception of the Olympian foundation myth.

artworks.title: Urn with the Killing of Myrtilus
artworks.description: This urnetta from the Hypogeum of the Volumnii (Perugia) again freezes Myrtilus' death: Pelops' betrayal of the charioteer who had helped him win. Etruscan funerary art repeats the scene as an emblem of broken faith — Hermes' son as the murdered helper whose last words damn a dynasty.

popCulture.title: Myrtoan Sea
popCulture.description: Greek geography named the sea south of Euboea after Myrtilus — the charioteer Pelops cast into the waves, a place-name that still remembers his fall.

popCulture.title: Pelops
popCulture.description: The Pelopid curse begins with Myrtilus' death — the charioteer's betrayal and murder that stains Atreus, Thyestes, and Agamemnon.
